BY UNITED STATES
AMERICAN NOTE TO GERMANY
DEMANDS REPARATION AND
NO REPETITION.
WILL PROTECT CITIZENS
Series of Incidents Cited in
Communication to Show Violation of
America's Rights - Note Cabled to .
Ambassador Gerard.
Washington. - The United States
government on May 13 cabled
Ambassador Gerard for presentation to the
German government a note calling
attention "to the grave situation which
has resulted" from violation of
American rights on the high seas,
culminating in the sinking of the Lusitania with
a loss of more than 100 American lives.

The communication expresses the
confident expectation of the United
States "that the imperial German
government will disavow the acts of which
the government of the United States
complains; that they will make
reparation so far as reparation is possible for
injuries which are without measure,
and that they will take immediate
steps to prevent the recurrence of
anything so obviously subverse of the
principles of warfare for which the
imperial government in the past so
wisely and so firmly contended.
In its conclusion, the note states that
"the imperial German government will
not expect the government of the
United States to omit any word or any
act necessary to the performance of
its sacred duty of maintaining the
rights of the United States and its
citizens and of safeguarding their free
exercise and enjoyment.

In view of recept acts of the
German authorities in violation of
American rights on the high seas, which
culminated in the torpedoing and
sinking of the British steamship Lusitania
on May 7, 1915, by which, over 100
American citizens lost their ihres, it is
clearly wise and desirable that the
government of the United tSates and the
imperial German government should
come to a clear and full understanding
as to the grave situation which has
resulted.
"The sinking of the British
passenger steamer Falaba by a German
submarine on March 28, through which
Leon C. Thrasher, an American
citizen, was drowned ; the attack on April
28 on the American vessel Cushing by
a German aeroplane ; the torpedoing on
May 1 of the American vessel
Gulflight by a German submarine, as a
result of which two or more American

citizens met their death; and finally
the torpedoing and sinking of the
steamship Lusitania, constitute a
series of events which t*he government
of the United States has observed
with growing concern, distress and
amazement.
Continuing the note enters into the
details of the submarine warfare, and
takes the German government to task
for the Lusitania disaster.

Ought to Back Up Demands
Made on Germany.
Jackson, Miss. - United States
Senator John Sharp Williams in a
statement regarding th# Lusitania disaster,
declared that if the vessel was armed

her, "but," he added, "I am informed

knew that the Lusitania was armed

she was on the last," he
continuedThat's a lie, because they have spies,

DESTROYER MAKES REPORT
Official Statement Is Given Out by
Berlin of How Lusitania Was
Torpedoed and Sunk.
Berlin. - From the report received
from the submarine which sank the
Lusitania the following official version
qf the incident is published by the
admiralty staff under the signature of
Admiral Behncke:
"The Submarine sighted the
steamer which showed no flag May 7 at
2:20 o'clock Central European time,
afternoon, on the southeast coast of
Ireland, in fine, clear weather.

At 3:10 one torpedo was fired at
the Lusitania, which hit her
starboard side below the captain's bridge.
The detonation of the torpedo was
followed immediately by a further
explosion of extremely strong effect.
The ship quickly listed to starboard
and began to sink.
"The second explosion must be
traced back to the ignition of
quantities of ammunition inside the ship."

Merchantman Destroys Submarine.
Blyth, England. - A German
submarine is reported to have been sunk in
the North sea. The captain of the

London. - The French, who already

proved to be the graveyard of so
many thousands of men since the
opposing lines were established there
last autumn.

'The Germans claim to have made a
slight advance, but with the battle
ebbing and flowing, that is not
considered serious in military circles here. j

army has repulsed an attempt of the I
Germans to regain the bridge head J
which King Albert's forces established
on the right bank of the Yser canal,
while^down in the Woevre another
French army is pushing its offensive

Pretre, which would be a step nearer,
in the allies' aim to force the
Germans to evacuate St. Mihiel.

ANOTHER WARSHIP IS SUNK
British Battleship Goliath Is
Torpedoed in the Dardanelles - 500
British Sailors Lose Lives.
London. - The British battleship
Goliath has been torpedoed in the
Dardanelles. It is feared 500 have been
lost.
The British submarine E-14 has
penetrated through the Dardanelles and
into the Sea of Marmora, sinking two
Turkish gunboats and a Turkish
transport.
These announcements were made in
the house of commons May 13 by
Winston Churchill, first lord of the
admiralty.
While no definite information had
been received as to the number of
lives lost on the Goliath, Mr- Churchill
said he feared it would reach 500.

Twenty officers and 160 men of thf
Goliath's crew were saved.
Mr. Churchill said:
"The Goliath was torpedoed at night
in a torpedo attack by destroyers while
protecting the French flank just
inside the straits.
The admiral commanding at the
Dardanelles also telegraphs that the
submarine E-14, which, with so much
daring penetrated to the Sea of
Marmora, has reported that she sank two
Turkish gunboats and a large Turkish
transport.
The Goliath was one of the older
British battleships of the
pre-dread'naught type. She was built in 1898.

Her complement was 750 men. She
was 400 feet long on the water line,
displaced 12,950 tons, and was armed I
with four 12-inch and twelve 6-Inch
guns; twelve 12-pounders, six
3-pounders, two machine guns, and fouf
torpedo tubes.
The Goliath is the third British
battleship whose loss in the Dardanelles
attack has been announced by the
British government. Loss of the
Irresistible and Ocean was announced on
March 19. On April 5 a wireless
dispatch from Berlin said the British
battleship Lord Nelson also had been
destroyed. That report was not con
firmed.

ITALY FACES GRAVE CRISIS
Unable to Decide War Question, the
Cabinet Resigns - internal
Revolution Threatens.
London. - The Italian cabinet has
resigned.
"The council of ministers,
Reuter's Rome correspondent,
sidering that it did not possess the
unanimous assent of the
constitutional parties regarding its international
policy which the gravity of the
situation demands, has decided to hand its
resignation to the king. An official
note to this effect was issued May 14.
"The king has reserved his decision
as to whether the resignation will be
accepted."
The political parties whose policies
are in favor of Italy remaining
neutral have announced the intention of
organizing a demonstration to
counteract the actions of those who favor
intervention.

The police of Rome, fearing
conflicts between the citizens of the
various parties, are taking extraordinary
measures to cope with the situation.
Troops occupy - all the important
points of the city and are especially in
force in the vicinities of the
AustroHungarian and German embassies.
Strong detachments of soldiers also
are being kept in the neighborhood of
ex-Premier Giolittl's house ready to
rush to his defense if necessary.
Former Premier Giolitti, regarded
as the leader of the party opposed to
war, has published in the Tribuna a
letter declaring he came to Rome
because he was summoned here to
exercise his views. He says his
convictions have not changed since he ex
pressed them in a speech

LONDON, May 7. The steamer Lusitania, filled with
passenger, many of whom were Americans, was either torpedoed or blown up
by an infernal machine while off Old Head of Kinsale, at 2:33 this
afternoon. The latest reports received here say that all of the passengers were
saved.

Sinking of the Lusitania was the hardest blow of the war to date so
far as neutral commerce was concerned. The reports received here arc
fragmentary, but all agree that the big liner began calling for help by
her wireless at 2:33.
The first to pick her up was the wireless station at Landsend.
The appeal was urgent.
"We have a big list,; rush help," flashed through the air, and
immediately orders were sent to the nearest points to get every available craft
to the scene.

The German submarine which sunk the Lusitania is believed here
to be the same which yesterday sunk the two 5,000-ton freighters
Centurian and Candidate, and on Wednesday sunk the sailing ship Earl of
Latham.
The admiralty has sent a flotilla of fast destroyers to search for the
under-sea boat.
The fishing fleet from Kinsale was early on the scene and
immediately began the work of taking on board the passengers from the big
liner. It is understood that the Lusitania's own boats were used to care
for her passengers.

On all of her recent trips .these boats have been swung overside and
their covers removed, ready for any eventuality, and it is possible that
to this precaution may be due the salvation of the passengers.
The first word reaching London of the plight of the Lusitania was
an unconfirmed rumor received at the general offices of the Cunard line.
It said that the big steamer was in trouble. The line officials made
it public and promised to keep the public informed of everything that
happened. ,
There was much excitement. There had been grave doubt that
the Germans were in earnest when they threatened to attack the passenger-carrying
liners. I
The sinking of the Falaba had been considered the final act of this
kind, and when it was realize dthat the biggest passenger liner in
commission had fallen victim to the war London was aghast.

Wall Street Stunned,
But Reacts at Once
NEW YORK. May 7. Stunned by the sinking of the Lusitania the
stock market this afternoon suffered one of the severest reactions in
its history.
Prices dropped almost instantaneously three and four points.
Bethlehem Steel, a stock which has fluctuated sharply for several weeks,
was sold off 29 points, from the high of the day, to 130.
When the first report of the sinking of the big liner was received
on the floor traders threw large blocks of stock on the market for any
price that they would command. In the railroad issues the international
stocks were the weakest. Canadian Pacific declined more than seven
points. Northern Pacific lost over four points. Southern Pacific went
down three full points.

The selling was general throughout the list, but strange to say
when a confirmation of the disaHter had been received several of the
stocks which had suffered largest losses recovered in part.

PORTUGAL IS IN
THROESOF REVOLT
REVOLUTIONARY PARTY
OVERTHROWS GOVERNMENT AND
SELECTS PRESIDENT.
MANY KILLED IN FIGHTING
Order Is Partly Restored When Chagas
Is Proclaimed
President - Leaders New Order Want a
National Government.

Lisbon. - The success of tlie
revolutionary forces has been confirmed.
The new government, which will be
presided over by Jacob Chagas, was
proclaimed from the windows of the
city hall, and the announcement was
received with enthusiasm
manifestation.
The military governor of Lisbon
immediately posted throughout the city
proclamation praising the courage of
the citizens and calling on civilians
to deliver up all arms at the arsenal
under pain of arrest.
Casualties in the fighting of May 14
numbered 67 killed and 300 wounded.
The insurgents wrecked and looted
the house in which Capt. Couceiro, the
Royalist leader, stayed until recently.

Several Royalists were arrested,
including Marquis Ficalho.
Order has been restored partly, and
the new government is taking
measures to re-establish normal conditions.
The former minister of marine was
arrested and taken aboard a warship
for having ordered a destroyer to sink
warships bombarding tlie city. News
from Oporto indicates that the
disturbances there were similar to those
in Lisbon, but that there were fewer
casualties.
All the regiments in Lisbon and in
th& provinces now have surrendered.
The last to capitulate were cavalry
regiments which led the military move
ment resulting in the appointment of
Pimenta Costa as premier in January.

A proclamation issued by the
revolutionary committee in Lisbon says:
"We are going to restore the
repuhlto-ta tl)e republicans. We demand
a national government and
consequently it ought to be republican.
We shall adopt no party flag, because
we wish all republicans to be united
for the dignity of the country, and the
salvation of the republic.
"We do not advise* violence or
reprisals. Our energy does not preclude
generosity for the vanquished. It is
the province of the national
government alone to execute measures for
patriotic defense. All may rely upon
its honor and its patriotism."

issued May 16 show 92 British officers
killed, 204 wounded and 62 missing.
Among the officers killed w*ere
Brig.Gen. Arthur Willoughby,' G. Lowry
and Capt. the Hon. Eric Edward

Anti-German Feeling Intense.
London. - Never since the war
began has such a wave of anti-German
feeling surged through the country as
at the present t|me. It is due entirely
to the sinking of the Lusitania.
Workmen are refusing to labor
alongside of men of German birth,
whether naturalized or not. In many
towns premises occupied by Germans
have been damaged or destroyed, and
even the exchanges in London and
provincial towns are barring the doors
to persons of German blood.
There have been riots in Liverpool,
Manchester, Sanford and Birkenhead.

In Liverpool Germans have been
interned and those who are naturalized
subjects of Great Britain have been
advised to go to interior towns or seek
internment.
Offers Reward for Bodies.
Queenstown. - The Cunard company
has offered a reward of $5 each for
the recovery of bodies of the
Lusitania victims, and the American
government supplemented this offer by
another of an equal sum for the body
of each American found.

FRENCH ADVANCE SLOWLY
Push the Germans Hard in Effort to
Break Through Lines on the
St. Mihiel Wedge.
London. - The French, who already
have gained possession of what was
thought to be impregnable German
positions north of Paris, are reported to
be continuing their victorious advance,
while the British are asserted to be
holding a large force of Germans in
their front and repulsing all German
attempts to reach Ypres, which has
proved to be the graveyard of so
many thousands of men since the
opposing lines were established there
last autumn.

The Germans claim to have made a
slight advance, but with the battle
ebbing and flowing, that is not
considered serious in military circles here.
Along toward the coast the Belgian
army has repulsed an attempt of the
Germans to regain the bridge head
which King Albert's forces established
on the right bank of the Yser canal,
while down in the Woevre another
French army is pushing its offensive
and claims to have gained possession
of the whole of the forest of Le
Pretre, which would be a step nearer
in the allies' aim to force the
Germans to evacuate St. Mihiel.

The Austro-Germans after their
lightning-like rush through Western
Galicia, now have reached a line
running due north and south to the west
of Przemysl, while the other armies,
emerging from the Carpathians, are
pressing the Russian flank. Even up
in Poland it is asserted that the
victory of the Teutonic allies in tire south
has had the effect of forcing the Rus
sians to fall back.

ANOTHER WARSHIP IS SUNK
British Battleship Goliath Is
Torpedoed in the Dardanelles - 500
British Sailors Lose Lives.
London - The British battleship
Goliath has been torpedoed in the
Dardanelles. It is feared 500 have been
lost.
The British submarine E-14 has
penetrated through the Dardanelles and
into the Sea of Marmora, sinking two
Turkish gunboats and a Turkish
transport.
These announcements were Tnade in
the house of commons May 13 by
Winston Churchill, first lord of the
admiralty.
While no definite information had
been received as to the number of
lives lost on the Goliath, Mr- Churchill
said he feared it would reach 500.

Twenty officers and 160 men of the
Goliath's crew were saved.
Mr. Churchill said:
"The Goliath was torpedoed at night
in a torpedo attack by destroyers while
protecting the French flank just
inside the straits.
"The admiral commanding at the
Dardanelles also telegraphs that the
submarine E-14, which, with so much
daring penetrated to the Sea of
Marmora, has reported that she sank two
Turkish gunboats and a large Turkish
transport."
The Goliath was one of the older
British battleships of the
pre-dread'naught type. She was built in 1898.

Her complement was 750 men. She
was 400 feet long on the water line,
displaced 12,950 tons, and was armed
with four 12-inch and twelve 6-inch
guns; twelve 12-pounders, six
3-pounders, two machine guns, and four
torpedo tubes.
The Goliath is the third British
battleship whose loss in the Dardanelles
attack has been announced by the
British government. Loss of the
Irresistible and Ocean was announced on
March 19. On April 5 a wireless
dispatch from Berlin said the British
battleship Lord Nelson also had been de
stroyed. That report was not cod
firmed.

Washington. - The United States
government on May 13 cabled
Ambassador Gerard for r.resen.Utica
German government a note calling
attention "to the grave situation which
has resulted" from violation of
American rights on the high seas,
culminating in the sinking of the Lusitania with
a loss of more than 100 American lives.
The communication expresses the
confident expectation of the United
States "that the imperial German
government will disavow the acts of which
the government of the United States
complains; that they will make
reparation so far as reparation is possible for
injuries which are without measure,
and that they will take immediate
steps to prevent the recurrence of
anything so obviously subverse of the
principles of warfare for which the
imperial government in the past so
wisely and so firmly contended."

In its conclusion, the note states that
"the imperial German government will
not expect the government of the Unit-,
ed States to omit any word or any
act necessary to the performance of
its sacred duty of maintaining the
rights of the United States and its
citizens and of safeguarding their free
exercise and enjoyment."
"In view of recent acts of the
German authorities in violation of
American rights on the high seas, which
culminated in the torpedoing and
sinking of the British steamship Lusitania
on May 7, 1915, by which over 100
American citizens lost their lives, it is
clearly wise and desirable that the
government of the United tSates and the
imperial German government should
come to a clear and full understanding
as to the grave situation which has
resulted.

"The sinking of the British
passenger steamer Falaba by a German
submarine on March 28, through which
Leon C. Thrasher, an American
citizen, was drowned; the attack on April
28 on the American yessel Cushing by
a German aeroplane; the torpedoing on
May 1 of the American yessel
Gulflight by a German submarine, as a
result of which two or more American
citizens met their death; and finally
the torpedoing and sinking of the
steamship Lusitania, constitute a
series of events which the government
of the United States has observed
with growing concern, distress and
amazement.

DESTROYER MAKES REPORT
Official Statement Is Given Out by
Berlin of How Lusjtania Was
Torpedoed and Sunk.
Berlin. - From the report received
from the submarine which sank the
Lusitania the following official version
of the incident is published by the
admiralty staff under the signature of
Admiral Behncke:
"The submarine sighted the
steamer which showed no flag May 7 at
2:20 o'clock Central European time,
afternoon, on the southeast coast of
Ireland, in fine, clear weather.

"At 3:10 one torpedo was fired at
the Lusitania, which hit her
starboard side below the captain's bridge.
The detonation of the torpedo was
followed immediately by a further
explosion of extremely strong effect.
The ship quickly listed to starboard
and began to sink.
"The second explosion must be
traced back to the ignition of
quantities of ammunition inside the ship."

New York. - The setting of the
great naval war, to be played
somewhere off the Atlantic coast this
week, has been about completed,
while the defending fleet lies in the
Hudson river awaiting the grand
review by President Wilson. Four
vessels of the auxiliary division which
is to compose part of Rear Admiral

steaming toward an unrevealed

May 13.
Mobilization of the Atlantic fleet

arrival of three divisions of the
torpedo flotilla, which anchored in
column along the New Jersey.side of

nations"We also charge the officers of said

American captain and members of Its
crew, offer an eloquent commentary
of the actual working of the theory
that force is not necessary to assert
rights and that a policy of blood
andiron can with efficacy be met by a
policy of milk and water."
"I think that China is entitled ta

fight.'

Among the land bargains in sight
today none exceed those of central
South Dakota. In the heart of this
territory is Hand county, with one
half her lands waiting for the hand
and brain of man to be made into
farms.
This "raw" land is scattered about
in all parts of the county, with
developed farms close bv. The man
who buys and improves one of these
tracts of land is not on the frontier,
nor is he surrounded by claim
shanties. He is in the midst of a
tolerably well developed locality, with
schools, churches, telephones,
markets. and very well improved farms.

This raw land is largely held by
non-resident speculators. It is not
moving fast enough to suit many of
the owners. They are now
purchasable at bargains - and here is the
whv:

School land, unimproved, sold in
fifteen counties of South Dakota this
spring at an average of $58,24 per
acre. The average price in Miner
countv was $64 98. For actual use
very few farmers of Hand county
would trade their farms, acre for
acre, for Miner countv land. True,
the land of that county will sell for
more today than the land of Hand
countv, but the difference is not in
the soil, or climate, or crops
produced. Miner countv is 42 miles east of
Hand, and consequently that much
nearer the thicker settlements and
more generally developed localities.

Twenty years ago Miner countv was
exactly in the class of Hand county.
The hot winds and poor wheat crops
of those days were similar in the two
counties, and brought similar results,
viz: dissatisfied and discontented
people, hundreds moved awav, both
counties went populist, and land
could hardlv be given awav.

This was followed by slow
development. changing of methods,
accumulation of resources by mixed
farming, stock raising, dairying, etc.
So far the two counties have had
almost the same experience, with
the exception that more farmers
have returned to Miner county, and
more farms were developed Hand
eountv raw land is cheaper simply
because there more of it. Today
there is very close to one farm to
each 640 acres of land in this county.
A very conse-valive estimate is that
our farm population can be doubled,
with a developed farm to each half
section of land. And in many
countries 320 acres of land would be
a principality.

Hand county's raw land is cheaper
today than it will ever be auain.
The people now living here and
occupying only one half the land, are
just beginning to reap the profits of
an established business with
sufficient capital or resources with which
to conduct that business. The
pioneer of the frontier seldom makes
profits, because he has no capital or
resources It takes a generation of
patient toil to acquire vhat he
lacked to begin with. But the man who
comes in now with sufficient capital
to buy land and do business on a
farm will go forward with the
second generation of development.

Hand eountv wants more settlers
on her farms-at least double her
present number. She offers the
last opportunity to buy land at first
generation prices in a locality
already in the stages of second
generation development.

In 1915 farming is a business
the best and most profitable
business in America if capital and
resources be exactly compared.
Twelve years ago the Press told
j*s readers that Hand county land
was ' a good buy". Starting at
two or three dollars an acre it
rushed up to $25 to S4O in the next few
years. A few slacK years, however,
coupled with coming due mortgages,
have caused a desire of some land
holders to let go - even to the
extent of sacrificing something.
Today there are a number of first class
bargains in sight in Hand county,
and the sig.is of the times look as if
these bargains are good buys in

Members of 1915 Class Present
"Maneuvers of Jane"
Th? Miller High School Senior
Class gave their annual play entitled
"The Maneuvers of Jane", on
Friday evening at the opera house to a
fine large crowd, and the audience
was very appreciative, and with the
voung people from beginning to
end. It is probably the best plav
from every standpoint ever given by
a Miller high school class.
In the first place good judgement
was shown in the character of the
play. It was full of healthfull tun.
and the too frequent and drinking
and smoking scenes in such
entertainments were conspicious by their
absence. This is commendable.

The credit for the splendid training
that the class showed, is due to Mrs
Glen M. Waters, who was
painstaking and careful in the training.
The marks of efficiency
and-carcfulness were seen all through the play.
The class is fortunate in having
training bv one of such ability and
judgement. This was manifest in
the selection of the parts to fit the
actors. It was more than noticeable
that each actor had a part that was
natural to him. And again the play
itself was not too old for plavers,
neither was it too tragical. The
comedv of it was healthfully
humorous. It finely illustrated the old
oroverb that "The course of true
love never did run smooth".
Altogether the effect was pleasing,
and the trainers and members of
the class are rcallv to be
congratulated, and commended.

"The Maneuvers of Jane" were
certainly interesting and very
human. She was a young girl
who was sent awav to boarding
school and she. of course, fell in love
with a young man whom her father
was not in love with, and there was
a clash in Jane's and father's
judgment about the young man. This
resulted in scheming, and some
escapades of an innocent nature on the
par* of Jane and her lover. Finally
Jane won out, and father
surrendered all the while protesting that he
had not given his consent, yet giving
it. And so for Jane and George
"all's well that ends well." "They
lived happily ever afterward,"
probably in California.

Miss Jean Garrett, the class
valedictorian, was "Jane", and
acquitted herself with credit, a better
impersonator it would be hard to find.
She put her whole soul in to all she
said and did. Her part was worthy
of the valedictorian.
And the same is true of Carl
Mover, the salutatonan of the class,
who impersonated "Lord Bapchild".
All the while we was being so hotly
pursued by the young lady who had
her heart ret on him, he was so
gentlemanly, and polite, that he could
hardly sav his soul was his own. But
it didn't seem to be, for he admitted
that his proposal to Miss Constantia
Gage was "an accident". Carl was
fine all through.

George Kenadv showed himself a
real actor. He had a long and
difficult part as "Jervis Punshon". and
he sustained his part extremely well
all through. George deserves to be
amoung the "first honors" in his
w'ork.

first class in her part. She was
popular with the audience, and was

"Jane". Erdine Berry believed
that "a bird in the hand was worth
two in the bush", and so she 'took
no chances", but held on with a life
and death grip.
Hazel Schmieter as "Pamela" was
a regular sleuth, always being on

discomfort to those whom she was
worrying. But they finally dropped
ber by strategy, and they went
their way rejoicing in the loss of

Beatrice Williams was a very

The big Cunard liner, Lusitania,
Hying the British Hag. was torpedoed
Friday, off the Irish coast, and went
down. Some 1200 peop'e are
reported lost. The vessel was one of
the largest alloat. Its length was
790 feet, and width 88 feet. It
would reach from the Vanderbilt
hotel to the opera house, and almost
as wide as Miller's main street.
Before the ship sailed advertisements
appeared in New York papers
warning the public that the Lusitania
would lie torpedoed in English
waters. The German
announcement that she would blockade Great
Britian with her submarines was not
taken seriously at first, because of
Britian's great fleet and her rule
of the sea, but the Germans have
sent manv boats of one kind or
ananother to the bottom during the
past few weeks, and so far Great
Britain seems unable to stop the
destruction.

Justice Hughes Not a Candidate
What is purported to be an
authoritative statement was published
in Washington papers recently
declaring that Justice Charles Hughes
would not be a candidate for the
republican nomination for president.
Under existing conditions he was
thought by many tj be the most
available man among those
mentioned for the honor. His decision is
doubtless a wise one from a personal
standpoint. He holds a position on
the supreme bench which is onlv
second** to that of president, It is
removed from the turmoil and
uncertainties of polities, and he may
hold it for life It is said that
President Taft would have
preferred a like position instead of the
presidency. It w«»s also said at the
time that President Taft appointed
Mr Hughes to the supreme bench io
get a strong opbutient out the wav

for his own renomination.
However. politics is one of the most
peculiar and excentric things the
human family entertains itself with.
A condition which appears to be
exactly right for n certain individual
one year may be entirely changed
the next. Likewise a man scarcely
considered todav mav be the one
individual to fit the conditions and
times a year later. This is readily
corroborated by the history of both
the old parties. President Wilson,
himself unknown to the political
world, quickly shelved men like
Brvan. Clark and Underwood.

President Haves beat out men like
Blaine and Conkling, and President
Garfield liecame a successful
candidate over night, against such
prominent men as Grant, Blaine and
Sherman

Japan and China Agree
The threatened war between Japan
and China has been averted. Japan
put up a big demand upon several
points. China refused to comply.
Japan modified her demands
somewhat, and the Chinese government
accepted to avoid war. When the
rest of the world has time to
look into the matter, it will
probably be discovered that Japan will
control China.

Increased Acreage Sown
Five per cent more oats, three per
cent more barley, and one and a
third per cent more wheat sown in
Hand county this spring than last, is
the declaration of local elevator
men. They obtain their estimate
from thirty farmers scattered over
the county. The late season may
lessen the corn acreage a trifle, but
it is too early to determine that, as
some kinds of corn may be planted
here as late as the middle of June.

White House Declines
to Comment on Sinking
President Wilson had just finished lunch when he was
informed by Assistant Secretary Forster of the press
dispatches telling of the sinking of the Lusitania.
Just before that he had been holding a conference
with Charles R. Crane, of Chicago, whp is expected to sail
for Europe May 22 on a special mission for the Persident.
Before that the President had been conferring with
his Cabinet regarding the attack on the, American steamer
Gulflight by German submarine last week.

No comment was made at the White House, in
absence of any official confirmation, the State and Navy
Department having advised the White House that their only
information was that given them by the newspaper men.
That the Lusitania would be attacked on her arrival
in the war zone has been the one big fear of the
Administration. It was thought the action of the German
embassy in publishing an advertisement last week warning

the Americans not to go abroad on the Lusitania
foreshadowed an attack on that vessel.
Regardless of this warning and the receipt of a
number of anonymous telegrams of a similar character, scores

of Americans, including men, women, and children,
decided to take their chances.
It is admitted in Administration circles that if any of
these Americans have been killed by the attack on the
Lusitania the situation will be the most critical faced by
the United States Government since the outbreak of the
war.
Confronting officials is the plain threat contained in
the American protest against the war zone decree of
Germany that if any American lives were lost in submarine
attacks upon merchant vessels the United States would
take measures to safeguard its interests, regarding such an
attack as "an unfriendly act."
Following the receipt of the information conveyed to
him by Mr. Forster the President did not leave the White
House for his customary afternoon game of golf.

One suggestion thrown out in offichl circles was to
the effect that if no American lives wre lost the attack on
the Lusitania might serve a good purpose in dissuading
Americans from taking unnecessary risk by persisting in
going abroad in the ships cf belligerent nations for
purposes of pleasure. Some time ago Secretary Bryan
issued a formal statement in which he urged Americans ret
to go abroad and visit, belligerent countries on mere
sightseeing tours.

To Blow Up Lusitania

Navy Department officials first heard of the attack
on the Lusitania this, afternoon through the press
dispatches. Prominent officials of the department said they had
expected the Lusitania would be sunk, but had thought it
would be blown up from the inside. They expected an
attempt on the Lusitania similar to the one made not long
ago to blow up the French liner La Touraine.
These officials said they would have been less
surprised at an attempt to destroy the vessel from within than
they were at the submarine attack. They admitted they
had believed the warnings conveyed to passengers on the
Lusitania before the vessel sailed pointed to a well defined
plan to destroy her.

More than fifteen hundred persons, American citizens
among the number, were lost yesterday, it is feared, when the.
big Cunard liner Lusitania was Vrpcdoed ofT Old Head of
Kinsale. Ireland, by a Gerjnan submarine. The attack was
made without warning. The ship sank within fifteen
minutes. Two torpedoes are said to have been fired, both of

wnicn burst inside the big liner.
Out of a total number of 2,101 persons aboard, passengers
and crow with 187 American citizens, GOO were landed at
Queenstown. Others are said to have been brought into
Kinsale, Galley Head and Clonakilty. A late bulletin
received by the Cunard company expressed the belief that no
more than 500 or 600 were saved. Among the survivors, it is
reported, are many wounded, who have been taken to the
Naval Hospital at Queenstown. This indicates that the
explosion must have been extremely violent or that there was :i
second interior explosion.

Alfred G. Vanderbilt is reported to have been lost in
the disaster. , Capt. W. T. Turner of the liner was saved.
One hundred bodies were brought into Queenstown. It
was stated that this number of persons taken from the
Lusitania after the explosion died of injuries or exposure on the
way to'land. Many of the survivors were badly hurt, scores
of them being unable to walk. Rome of the Americans among

The Lusitania was struck around 2:15 o'clock in the
afternoon (Irish time 0:15 A. M. New York time), ju.-t
before rounding into the entrance of St. George's Chan'n"!.
She was about ten miles south by west off Old Head of
Kinsale at the time, apparently proceeding at her top speed.
The blow must have been terrific. Her wireless
operator barely had time to send a distress message. The marim!
observer at Old Head just made out the big ship with a heavy
list when she disappeared. Twenty lifeboats and rafts were
left Iloating on the water.

Scores of other boats, fishermen, a Greek steamship,
motor boats, lifeguard boats and tugs were rushed from every
port fr oni Queenstown south to Galley Head. It is fairlv
certain that of the lifeboats and rafts of the Lusitania
capable of carrying 2,605 persons only a little more than one-half
were available because of the careening of the ship.
The disaster to the Lusitania was clearly forecast by the.
German Government both in this country and abroad. Just
before the ship sailed last Saturday morning the GerniMp
Embassy had caused an advertisement to be printed
broadcast warning all Americans to keep off British ships sailing
into the war zone.

Gen. Smith's Military Record.

Following is a summary of the
military record of General Joseph S.
Smith, of Bath, Maine (now of Bangor.
Maine,) during the Civil War,
Entered the service as a private. 3rd
Maine Infantry, May 30. 1861;
mustered in June 4th. 1861; gradually
promoted to be corporal, sergeant,
lieutenant, captain, lieutenant colonel,
colonel etc. to his present rank of
brevet brigadier general U. S.
Volunteers.
Served as Aide-de-Camp on the
staffs of Generals Hancock. Sedgwick.
Couch. Humphreys, Howard and
Warren. from each of whom he has
received highly complimentary letters.

Was Chief Commissary of the Army
of the Potomac months at a time
upon the staff of Major General Meade.
Engaged in the first battle of Bull
Run and nearly every battle of the ^nd
Corps up to and including the
surrender of Gen. Lee at Appomattox.
Promoted for 'gallantry in action".
Awarded a medal of honor by
Congress for "special bravery in battle
it Hatchers Run, Virginia, October
27, 1864." Recaptured two pieces of
artillery in that battle. Honorable
mustered out July 11. 1865, having
served in the army more than four
years, - in fact from the
commencement until the close of the Rebellion.

London, May 8. - 4.54 A. M. - A Dublin dispatch to the Exchange
Telegraph Co., says that the latest reports indicate the loss of life on the
Lusitania as more than 1000.
The Times Queenstown correspondent says that some of the
survivors who have arrived there report that Alfred Gwynne Vanderbilt
was drowned.

The Central News says that the number of the Lusitania's
passengers who died of injuries while being taken to Queenstown will reach
100. Captain Turner of the Lusitania was among those saved.
The Dublin Times states that the survivors aboard the tug
Stormcock all are in a deplorable condition and that some of them are
wounded. Twenty-two of those who were landed here have since died
of their injuries. Nearly a!! the officers except Capt Turner and the
first and second officers perished. The admiralty reports 590 persons
landed at Quenstown with 40 dead.

Queenstown, May 8. - 4.28 A. M. - Survivors of the Lusitania who
have arrived here estimate that only about 650 of those aboard the
steamer were saved and only a small proportion of those rescued were
saloon passengers.
A dispatch to the state department early today from American
Consul Frost at Queenstown stated that the total number of survivors
of the Lusitania was about 700.
London, May 8. - The Cunard liner Lusitania, which sailed out of
New York last Saturday with more than 2000 souls aboard, lies at the
bottom of the ocean off the Irish coast.. She was sunk by a German
submarine, which sent two torpedoes crashing into her side, while the
passengers, seemingly confident that the great swift vessel could elude
the German under-water craft, were having luncheon.

STRUCK BY TWO TORPEDOES
The Lusitania was steaming along about 10 miles off Old
Head, Kinsale, on the last leg of her voyage to Liverpool, when
about 2 o'clock in the afternoon a submarine suddenly
appeared, .and, so far as all reports go fired two torpedoes without
| warning at the steamer. One struck the bow and the other in
the engine room, causing terrific explosions. Almost
immediately great volumes of water poured through the openings and
the Lusitania listed.
Boats, which were already swung out on the davits, were
dropped overboard and were speedily filled with the passengers
who had been appalled by the attack.

A wireless call for help was sent out and immediately
rescue boats of all kinds were sent out both from the
neighboring points along the coast and Queenstown.
But within IS minutes, as (me survivor estimated, and
certainly within half an hour, the Lusitania had disappeared.
